stages.name: Economic growth: benefits and costs
stages.title: Economic growth: benefits and costs
stages.sub: Explain who gains from growth, how it lifts living standards, and why too much of it can backfire.

steps.q: A country's real output rises 3% this year. Workers' wage packets buy more than before. What has happened to what they can afford to buy?
steps.right: They can afford more, their real income has risen
steps.wrong: They can afford the same, only prices have risen
steps.hint: Output is genuinely higher, not just prices.

steps.q: As the economy grows, new firms enter and existing ones develop new product lines. Does the range of things on sale to buy tend to shrink or grow?
steps.right: It grows, with more choice and often better quality
steps.wrong: It shrinks, as firms focus on fewer products
steps.hint: Think about a growing economy attracting new firms and new versions of products.

steps.q: Households are spending more as the economy grows. What happens to firms' revenues, and what can they now afford to do with the extra money?
steps.right: Revenues and profits rise, giving firms more to invest
steps.wrong: Revenues and profits fall, forcing firms to cut back
steps.hint: More spending in the economy means more sales for firms.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Consumers have higher real incomes, more choice, and firms are investing more. Someone living on very little before now has more to spend on food, housing and healthcare. What tends to happen to their material standard of living, and to the number of people in absolute poverty?
steps.right: Living standards rise and absolute poverty tends to fall
steps.wrong: Living standards stay the same and poverty is unaffected
steps.hint: Put the three benefits together: more income, more choice, more investment. What do they add up to for people day to day?

steps.q: Actual output grows faster than the economy's potential, pushing it into a positive output gap with a boom building. Firms cannot produce fast enough to meet all the extra spending. What tends to happen to prices, and so to what people's incomes can actually buy?
steps.right: Prices are pulled up, eroding real incomes
steps.wrong: Prices stay stable since spending is rising for good reason
steps.hint: If demand outruns what firms can actually produce, what happens when everyone competes for the same limited output?
